title: Surviving on a Student Budget
focus: Phrasal verbs (run out of, cut down on, put aside, pass on, add up)

lines.text: Welcome to Smart Money. Today we're helping students who are always running out of cash before the end of the month.
I've been there. My first year, I used to spend my whole grant in the first week.
What went wrong?
I never kept track. Now I write down everything I spend, which helped me cut down on takeaways.
How much did you save?
Roughly eighty pounds a month. I put it aside in a separate account so I couldn't touch it easily.
Isn't that hard to do when prices keep going up?
It is. But small changes add up. For example, I stopped buying coffee every day and bought a flask instead.
What about big expenses, like textbooks?
Never buy new if you can avoid it. Check second hand shops, or ask older students to pass theirs on.
And if you run out of money anyway?
Don't panic and don't ignore it. Talk to the university's advice service early. They often have emergency funds.
Any final tip?
Treat yourself occasionally. If you never enjoy anything, you'll give up the whole plan.

title: The Student Who Built a Water Filter
focus: Noun clauses (what I found out was ...) and past simple vs past continuous

lines.text: Amina, you're sixteen and you've built a water filter that won your school science prize. How did it start?
My grandmother lives in a village where the tap water isn't always clean. I was visiting her when I noticed that she boiled every drop.
So you wanted a cheaper way?
Exactly. Boiling uses fuel, and fuel costs money. I started researching simple filters made of layers of sand, gravel and charcoal.
Did it work straight away?
Not at all. My first design was blocking within hours. What I found out was that the sand was too fine.
How did you fix it?
My teacher suggested adding a coarser layer on top. After that, the water ran much faster.
Is it safe to drink?
Not yet, and I want to be clear about that. The filter removes dirt, but it doesn't kill every germ, so boiling is still needed in some cases.
That's a very honest answer.
Science depends on honesty. If I exaggerated, someone could get ill.
What's next?
I'm testing it with a local laboratory, and I'd like to give the design away for free once it's proven safe.

title: Passwords That Protect You
focus: Advice, sequencing (firstly, once, finally) and conditionals

lines.text: Good morning. Today's session is about protecting your online accounts, which is easier than most people think.
Firstly, let's talk about passwords. Many people use the same one everywhere. If a criminal obtains it from one website, they can try it on all your other accounts.
Instead, you should use a different password for each important account. That sounds impossible, which is why a password manager is useful.
A password manager stores them safely, so you only need to remember one strong password.
Make that one long. A sentence of several unrelated words is harder to guess than a short word with symbols.
Secondly, switch on two step login wherever it's offered. Once it's active, a thief needs your phone as well as your password.
Thirdly, be suspicious of messages that create panic. A message saying your account will close today unless you click a link is almost always a trick.
When in doubt, don't click. Go to the official website by typing the address yourself.
Finally, keep your devices updated. Updates often fix security holes that criminals know about.
None of this is perfect, but together these habits make you a much harder target.
For next time, check which of your accounts offer two step login and switch it on.
Questions? Please send them to me by email before Friday.

title: The Night Market Report

lines.text: It's Friday night, and the old car park has been transformed into a street food festival. The air smells of garlic and grilled corn.
Welcome! Everything here is cooked in front of you, so there are no surprises.
You sell dumplings. What's the secret?
Fresh dough, made every morning. People are often surprised by how simple the filling is. It's the freshness that makes the difference.
The crowds are huge. Is it exhausting?
Very tiring, but exciting too. I'm usually exhausted by midnight, though I'm never bored.
Do customers ever complain?
Sometimes about the waiting time. But the queue moves quickly, and most people find it entertaining to watch us cook.
There's a real mix of food here.
That's the beauty of it. Neighbours from different countries share their family recipes, and visitors are amazed by the choice.
Is it hard to make a living?
It's seasonal. In winter, trade is disappointing, so I work at a restaurant. Summer pays for the rest of the year.
And what do you enjoy most?
Seeing a shy customer try something new and come back for more. That's rewarding.

title: Too Many Tourists?
focus: Contrast (on the one hand, on the other hand, whereas, while, meanwhile)

lines.text: Tonight's topic: can small towns survive without tourists, and can they survive with too many? Elias?
On the one hand, tourism brings jobs. In Marwick, one in three people work in hotels, cafes or boat tours.
On the other hand, those jobs are often seasonal and badly paid, whereas the rents keep rising for everyone.
Rents rise because of demand for housing, not only tourism. While I accept that holiday flats are a problem, a ban would hurt owners who depend on them.
Meanwhile, locals can't find homes. Young people who grew up here are being forced to leave.
So regulate it. Limit the number of holiday rentals, but don't punish tourists themselves.
I'd go further and charge a small entry fee on peak days, which would fund public services.
A fee might discourage some visitors, although it could also improve their experience, with fewer crowds.
That's possible. Still, the main aim should be a town people can live in, not just visit.
So you agree on limits but not on how strict. Thank you both.

title: A Farewell to Mrs Doyle
focus: Reflecting on the past (used to, would, past perfect)

lines.text: Good evening, everyone. I'm honoured to say a few words for Mrs Doyle, who retires today after thirty years at this school.
When I joined, I was terrified. I had never taught before, and she was the first person who made me feel welcome.
She used to leave a cup of tea on my desk before every parents' evening. She never mentioned it. She simply did it.
Her classroom was famous for its noise, though. Pupils would be debating, singing, or building something out of cardboard.
She believed that children learn best when they're curious, not when they're afraid.
Many of you here tonight were taught by her, and I'm sure you remember the day she brought a live chicken into a history lesson.
Don't ask me why. Nobody ever got a proper explanation.
Over the years, she had seen the school change. The chalkboards disappeared, computers arrived, and the staff room moved twice.
Yet her approach hasn't changed at all: listen first, then teach.
Mrs Doyle, I wish I could say we'll manage without you. Honestly, we won't. But we'll try.
So please raise your glasses to thirty years of kindness, patience and a very surprised chicken.
To Mrs Doyle!

title: Never Too Late for the Piano
focus: Verb patterns (no point in -ing, no use -ing, worth -ing)

lines.text: Welcome to The Second Act. Adam, you started piano lessons at fifty one. Why then?
My daughter was learning, and I realised I had always wanted to play. There was no point in waiting any longer.
Was it embarrassing sitting with children?
At first, yes. But it's no use worrying about what people think. Most of them were encouraging.
What's harder for adults: finger skills or reading music?
Reading. Children pick it up like a language. As an adult, I find it worth practising for ten minutes every day instead of one long session.
Do you ever feel discouraged?
Often. After a bad week, I sometimes feel like giving up, but I remind myself that progress isn't a straight line.
Do adults have any advantage?
Yes. We're better at planning and we can see the point of boring exercises. Children get bored quickly.
What would you say to someone thinking about starting?
It's worth trying, even if you only play simple songs. You don't have to become a concert pianist to enjoy it.
And your goal?
To play one piece properly for my daughter's wedding, someday. She's only twelve, so I have plenty of time.

title: Digging Up the Past
focus: Past passive and past perfect passive

lines.text: Henry, last summer you spent two weeks at an archaeological dig. How did you get involved?
A friend told me that volunteers were needed. I'd never touched a trowel, but we were trained in a day.
What were you looking for?
A farmhouse that had been abandoned centuries ago. We found the outline of walls after a farmer's plough had turned up some broken pottery.
What was a typical day?
Up at six, then hours of digging with tiny tools. Everything we found was photographed, measured and recorded before it was moved.
Why so careful?
Because once a layer has been removed, it can't be put back. The position of an object tells you as much as the object itself.
Did you find anything exciting?
A small coin, which had been lost, we think, by a traveller. I felt a strange connection with that person.
Was there anything disappointing?
Most of what we dug up was ordinary: bones from meals, pieces of cooking pots. But that's the point, because ordinary life is what we know least about.
Would you go again?
Definitely. My back ached for days, but I've already been signed up for next summer.
